General.Description:
Delphine Beaumont's mother sang constantly: in the kitchen while cooking, in the car, humming under her breath during long silences. She sang in French, in Arabic, in Berber — sometimes all three in the same song, switching languages mid-phrase with the unconscious fluency of a woman who had grown up in the space between cultures and made that space her home.

Delphine, born in Lyon, growing up between her mother's Algerian family and her father's French Catholic one, did not always know what language she was hearing. She grew up to become a musicologist. She suspects this is not a coincidence.

Songs My Mother Sang is a memoir built around music — the songs themselves, their origins, their meanings in different linguistic and cultural contexts, and what they meant to one woman who carried them across a sea and kept singing them in a country that did not always want her voice. Beaumont interweaves musical analysis with family history, cultural theory with the intimate textures of a childhood defined by the particular warmth and particular difficulty of a bicultural household.

The book is also, at its heart, a love letter. To her mother. To the songs. To the complicated, irreplaceable gift of being raised between worlds.
